back: Structures that resist wave attack, such as sea walls, groynes, rip-rap (rock armour) and revetments.
Working with natural processes: beach nourishment, dune stabilisation and managed retreat.
Deliberately allowing the sea to flood or erode land and moving the line of defence inland; it can create habitat such as saltmarsh.
A plan that sets a policy for each stretch of coast in a sediment cell: hold the line, advance the line, managed realignment or no active intervention.
About 60 km from Flamborough Head to Spurn Head; soft boulder-clay cliffs, a long North Sea fetch, retreat of about 1.8 m a year, and longshore drift to the south.
Two rock groynes and a rock revetment protected the village; the beach grew, but erosion further down the drift near Cowden is reported to have increased.
Managed realignment: new embankments set back inland, so the sea floods farmland and creates intertidal habitat.
Cost against benefit, effect on the sediment cell and downdrift coast, sustainability with rising sea level, and fairness to people and habitats.
Benefit–cost ratio = value protected ÷ cost; a value above 1 means the benefit exceeds the cost.
